The Atlantic. Originally called The Atlantic Monthly, it was founded in 1857 in Boston as an influential American magazine of literature, politics, culture, and social commentary. The magazine reflects New England intellectual and abolitionist traditions. Early contributors included Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau, and Julia Ward Howe, the author of The Battle Hymn of the Republic, alongside other major figures of their era. The Atlantic published Oliver Wendell Holmes and Nathaniel Hawthorne and became a venue for literary establishment voices. The magazine became known for long-form journalism, essays on politics and culture, and serious fiction, typically avoiding celebrity journalism. The editorial stance has emphasized progressive politics, intellectual rigor, and humanistic values throughout its history. The Atlantic shifted to monthly publication and expanded its reach in the twenty-first century while maintaining its reputation for sophisticated political analysis. The magazine became famous for publishing important political essays, including defenses of abolition and contemporary debates on democracy and rights. As a publication, The Atlantic served as a forum for New England transcendentalist and progressive thought, published major nineteenth-century American writers, and provided a venue for serious political and cultural debate.
